Owners (collectively, the “PJM TOs”)3 move to dismiss and answer the Complaint filed by the

allocation methodology for regional transmission facilities and asks the Commission to require

PJM and the PJM TOs to abandon that methodology and reassign Maryland’s portion of the costs

in a manner that is contrary to the PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff (“PJM Tariff”).

           The Complaint is a generalized attack on the accepted cost allocation methodology veiled

in broad assertions about aggregate costs and unsupported allegations about future large load

interconnections. The Complaint proposes sweeping remedies that would overturn settled rates,

override established PJM Tariff provisions, and complicate PJM’s transmission planning process.

Without meeting the burdens of section 206 of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”), the MDOPC asks

the Commission to overturn an established cost allocation framework, which is both central to the

pro forma Tariff and the PJM Tariff and which has already been found to be just and reasonable.

Furthermore, the PJM TOs are already taking steps to mitigate the risk of potential cost shifts if

anticipated loads do not materialize, including in response to the Commission’s June 18, 2026,

show cause order directed at PJM and the PJM TOs (“Large Load Order”).5 Simply put, the

Complaint is procedurally and legally deficient, contains flawed assumptions, and seeks

I.     INTRODUCTION

       The PJM methodology to allocate the costs of transmission facilities developed to resolve

reliability needs has, for over a decade, allocated costs to beneficiaries consistent with the

Commission’s cost causation principles. It continues to strike the right balance between broad

regional benefits created by transmission system upgrades and identifiable benefits.

       MDOPC asks the Commission to upend this longstanding and broadly supported

framework based not on evidence of an unjust or unreasonable rate, but on generalized

dissatisfaction with recent cost allocation outcomes. According to MDOPC, the growth of large

loads outside of Maryland means Maryland customers should no longer bear transmission costs

allocated under the PJM Tariff Commission-approved methodology. Yet MDOPC identifies no

specific project, no specific cost allocation, and no specific tariff provisions that allegedly violate

the FPA. Instead, it asks the Commission to abandon settled cost allocation principles based on

speculation about future large load development and conclusory assertions regarding aggregate

transmission costs. The Complaint identifies no project-specific evidence showing a mismatch

between costs and benefits, no demonstration that the existing methodology violates cost causation

principles, and no basis for finding the existing rate unjust or unreasonable.

       The Commission has several independent bases to dismiss the Complaint. First, MDOPC

fails at the outset because the Complaint does not establish the prerequisite showing under FPA

section 206 that PJM’s existing cost allocation methodology is unjust and unreasonable. Rather

than provide a project-specific analysis of costs, benefits, or cost allocation results, MDOPC asks

the Commission to infer unlawfulness from aggregate cost figures from aggregated costs across


                                                  3
 three Regional Transmission Expansion Plan (“RTEP”) reliability windows.6 Second, MDOPC

also seeks inappropriate relief that would undermine the states’ abilities to address retail ratepayer

protection. Third, MDOPC failed to pursue alternative remedies available to it at the state level or

with PJM or the PJM TOs before filing the Complaint. Fourth, the Commission’s recent show

cause order in Docket No. EL26-67-000 effectively obviates the Complaint. Allowing the

Complaint to proceed at the same time would unnecessarily complicate PJM’s and the PJM TOs’

efforts to address the Commission’s concerns.

           Even if the Commission reaches the merits, the Complaint fares no better. MDOPC has

not shown that the existing methodology is unjust and unreasonable, and the record demonstrates

the opposite: PJM’s existing cost allocation framework remains fully consistent with the

Commission’s cost causation principles and has broad stakeholder support. As discussed herein

and in the Russo Affidavit, the Complaint relies on flawed logic and fails to demonstrate the

relationship between the purported risks of large loads and the continued use of PJM’s existing

cost allocation framework.7 Accordingly, if the Commission does not dismiss the Complaint, it

should deny it in its entirety and reject MDOPC’s proposed replacement rate. Moreover, the PJM

TOs and states have already developed retail customer protections through retail tariffs for large

load customers and Commission-filed bilateral agreements. In contrast, the remedies proposed by

MDOPC are contrary to Commission policy, impractical, and inappropriate, and would therefore

be unjust and unreasonable. Rather than remedying any demonstrated defect, MDOPC’s proposals

would unravel settled cost allocation principles, reassign costs contrary to the PJM Tariff, and

MDOPC’s remedies would shift costs contrary to the allocation required by the PJM Tariff,

violating the filed rate doctrine, rule against retroactive ratemaking, and Order No. 1000’s rule

requiring ex ante cost allocation. MDOPC’s remedies would also recreate the flaws that caused

PJM to shift from its previous violation-based cost allocation methodology, rely on generator

interconnection principles inapt for load interconnection, and create a more complex and siloed

transmission planning process.

        In short, the Complaint identifies no unlawful rate, no defective tariff provisions, and no

unjust or unreasonable practice, yet seeks sweeping changes to a Commission-approved

framework. The Commission should dismiss the Complaint or, alternatively, deny it on the merits.

II.     BACKGROUND

        A.       The PJM Cost Allocation Methodology for Regional Transmission Facilities

        PJM uses a hybrid methodology to allocate to load customers the costs of regional

transmission facilities caused by reliability needs. As discussed in the Russo Affidavit, reliability

needs, other than stability needs, addressed by Regional Facilities8 (i.e., required transmission

enhancements included in the RTEP) or Necessary Lower Voltage Facilities9 are allocated 50

percent based on a load-ratio share basis and 50 percent to transmission zones based on the

(3) A.C. or D.C. shunt reactive resources connected to either of those types of facilities; and (4) a Required
Transmission Enhancement included in the RTEP. PJM Tariffs, Sch. 12 § (b)(i).

            The load-ratio share allocates costs using a postage-stamp basis.13 In approving the load-

ratio share, the Commission observed “that high-voltage transmission facilities have significant

regional benefits that accrue to all members of the PJM transmission system [and the] postage-

stamp method recognizes these widespread, although difficult to quantify benefits, by allocating

costs to all parties within PJM’s integrated network.”14

            SBDFAX allocates costs based on modeling of how each load zone contributes to power

flow over new transmission facilities during steady-state conditions. The analysis is updated

annually to account for changes in use due to grid modifications, which enables the identification

over time of the “more specific benefits of projects.”15 The Commission explained that SBDFAX

allows for “the ability to reflect . . . changing beneficiaries of a transmission facility, as well as

eliminating the need to analyze each reliability violation and driver of a project separately.”16

            The Commission approved the hybrid methodology because it “incorporates both the

postage-stamp method and the [SBDFAX] method,” which the Commission found “represents a

reasonable balance of broad regional benefits and specifically identifiable benefits over time.”17

The load-ratio share covers the more difficult-to-quantify benefits and users as might change over

time whereas the SBDFAX portion accounts for beneficiaries of the project due to electrical

proximity to the facilities.18 In approving this hybrid methodology, the Commission reiterated its

long-standing ratemaking principle that “[r]atemaking is not an exact science” so it therefore “must

be free” within reason “to take into account all relevant public interests, both existing and

foreseeable.”19 The Commission continued to find the hybrid methodology as just and reasonable

in 2018 when it approved its use to allocate certain costs under a contested settlement.20

           B.        The Complaint

allocation methodology is unjust and unreasonable.21                 MDOPC contends that the hybrid

methodology violates the Commission’s cost causation principles by assigning substantial costs to

Maryland ratepayers for transmission upgrades associated with out-of-state large load

development from which Maryland receives little benefit.22 MDOPC also challenges continued

use of SBDFAX.

from PJM’s three most recent transmission expansion planning windows: 2022 RTEP Window 3

(“2022 W3”), 2024 RTEP Window 1 (“2024 W1”), and 2025 RTEP Window 1 (“2025 W1”).

MDOPC alleges that these three planning cycles collectively allocated approximately $2 billion in

transmission capital costs to Maryland, which will increase Maryland customer bills by

approximately $1.6 billion over the next decade.23

            MDOPC argues that these cost allocations are unjust and unreasonable because the load

growth driving the transmission upgrades is heavily concentrated in four non-Maryland PJM

zones.24 MDOPC alleges a mismatch between the purported assumptions underlying PJM’s cost

allocation methodology and the concentrated load growth, which results in costs being assigned to

support data center growth in other states.

were caused by data center load growth and credit costs for that growth back to transmission zones

after the refund effective date; (3) direct PJM to develop a revised methodology for allocating

            C.          The Large Load Order

            By the time MDOPC filed its Complaint, the Commission had already announced its plans

III.       MOTION TO DISMISS

           A.       MDOPC Failed to Meet Its Burden of Showing the Existence of an Unjust
                    and Unreasonable Rate or Practice.

           The Commission has long held that a party bringing a section 206 complaint “has a burden

to do more than make mere unsubstantiated allegations to warrant a hearing.”33 To avoid

dismissal, a complainant bears the burden to “present a prima facie case demonstrating the

unjustness, unreasonableness, or discriminatory nature” of the rate at issue.34 A prima facie case

requires “an adequate proffer of evidence”35 that goes beyond “broad and unsubstantiated

allegations.”36 A complainant establishes a prima facie case by (1) identifying clearly the action

it supports reliability, deliverability, operational flexibility, future use, and service to all customers.

customer or category-by-category cost allocation evaluations for integrated transmission facilities

subject to the Commission’s jurisdiction, which the courts and the Commission have repeatedly

and expressly rejected.236 As discussed below, the benefit of solving for all the of the need drivers

Christopher Russo is a Vice President in CRA’s Energy Practice. He advises domestic and
international clients in the energy and natural resources industries in the areas of investment
strategy and economic analysis, asset valuation, energy technology, and generation and
transmission development. His expertise covers energy markets in North America, Europe, the
Middle East, and worldwide.
Mr. Russo started the Energy practice from a team of six people, growing it to over sixty as the
Energy Practice Chair from 2012 through 2025 before returning to focus full-time on client work.
He has testified in disputes and regulatory matters on issues regarding the economics, planning,
operation, and manipulation of energy markets and has testified numerous times at trial in
numerous countries. Mr. Russo also served on the Board of Directors of Neuco, a Boston-based
company which provides software to enable AI and neural network control of thermal power plants.

Prior to joining CRA, Mr. Russo was a senior consultant with Cambridge Energy Research
Associates in Paris, and prior to that, owned his own energy consulting firm as well as working for
ABB Corporate Research in the US and Switzerland. He started his career at MIT as the Plant
Engineer for the campus cogeneration power plant, and later held an academic appointment as a
Visiting Scientist at the MIT Energy Laboratory where he investigated electricity technology and
energy policy.
